title: Dream.exe: Can a Video Generator Dream a Robot's Next Move?
hook: A video model that 'understands' physics should produce motion a robot can perform. Dream.exe runs generated videos through a real execution pipeline — and finds pretty isn't physical.
key_points: Video generators make compelling clips, but do their motions obey real-world physics?
Dream.exe turns a generated manipulation video into robot trajectories and executes them in simulation.
Execution success is a grounding signal that purely visual quality metrics can't provide.
Across 8 models and 101 tasks, several achieved real execution success — but visual quality poorly predicted executability.
content_html: Video generation models produce strikingly realistic clips, but their output lives entirely on-screen. Zhao and colleagues ask a sharper question: if a model has really internalized how the physical world works, the motion it depicts should be doable — translatable into actions a robot can carry out. They turn that into a concrete test.
extra_html: Dream.exe is a video-to-execution pipeline. Given a scene image and a task description, it has a model generate a manipulation video, converts the depicted motion into robot trajectories, and executes them in a physics simulator — yielding a pass/fail grounding signal that visual quality scores alone can't provide. The authors evaluate 8 models (frontier closed-source generators, open-source generators, and robot-specific models) across 101 hand-curated manipulation tasks at three levels of physical complexity, scoring visual quality, trajectory fidelity, and execution success. Encouragingly, several models achieve measurable execution success — evidence that priors learned from internet-scale video already encode meaningful physics. But the headline finding is a disconnect: visual quality is a poor predictor of executability, revealing a dimension of capability that standard visual benchmarks miss entirely. The benchmark is being open-sourced; see the arXiv link.

related.hook: Instead of learning only from real experience, DreamerV3 builds a world model and practices inside its own imagination — one fixed config, 150+ tasks.

choices.text: Visual quality is a poor predictor of whether the generated motion is actually executable
The most visually realistic models were always the most executable
No model produced any executable motion at all

flashcards.explanation_html: Several models achieved measurable execution success — generative priors encode some physics — but visual quality didn't predict executability, exposing a capability axis standard visual evals miss.

flashcards.prompt: Why does robot manipulation make a good test of a video model's physical understanding?
flashcards.back_html: If a model has truly internalized physical laws, the motion it depicts should translate into executable robot behavior — turning an abstract 'understands physics?' question into a concrete, measurable one.
